items.prompt: In sales, what is prospecting?

options.label: Delivering the product after the deal is signed
Finding potential buyers who might need what you sell
Negotiating the final price and terms with a confirmed buyer
Answering objections raised during a product demo

rubric: Prospecting is the search for potential buyers.
Distractors describe later stages: negotiation, objection handling and delivery.

items.prompt: What does it mean to qualify a lead?

options.label: Send the lead a price list and wait for a reply to see who responds
Give the lead a discount to speed up the decision
Add the lead to a mailing list for future offers
Check whether the lead has the need and means to buy

rubric: Qualifying checks fit: need, budget, authority and timing.
Other options are outreach or pricing actions, not checks of buying fit.

items.prompt: In the common BANT qualification framework, what do the letters stand for?

options.label: Buyer, Approval, Negotiation, Terms
Brand, Audience, Network, Trust
Budget, Authority, Need, Timeline
Budget, Advertising, Negotiation, Targets

rubric: BANT is Budget, Authority, Need, Timeline.
Other options are invented sales-sounding word sets.

items.prompt: Which stage of a sales conversation is mainly about asking questions to learn the buyer's situation and needs?

options.label: Follow-up invoicing
Objection handling
Discovery
Closing

rubric: Discovery is the questioning stage that uncovers needs.
Closing and objection handling come later and focus on commitment and concerns.

items.prompt: What is 'closing' in a sale?

options.label: The review of why a past customer stopped buying
The step of asking the buyer to commit and agree to buy
The first call used to introduce yourself to a lead
The process of removing cold leads from the pipeline

rubric: Closing is asking for the buyer's commitment.
Other options describe introductions, churn review and pipeline cleaning.

items.prompt: Which of these are typical stages in a basic sales pipeline? Select all that apply.

options.label: Negotiation
Product recall
Qualified lead
Quarterly payroll run

items.prompt: A rep finishes a demo. The buyer says, 'This looks useful, but it costs more than we planned to spend.' The rep wants to name what the buyer just raised. What is this called in sales?

options.label: A referral
A qualification
An objection
A closing signal

rubric: A concern that blocks a purchase, such as price, is an objection.
A closing signal shows readiness to buy, which this does not.

items.prompt: Why do reps ask open-ended questions such as 'How does your team handle this today?' during discovery?

options.label: They keep the call short by steering the buyer straight to the product demo
They get the buyer to describe their needs in their own words
They make it easy to get a quick yes or no that confirms the buyer is qualified
They push the buyer to agree to a price early in the call

rubric: Open questions draw out detailed information about needs.
Yes/no answers and early price talk are what open questions avoid.

items.prompt: A buyer says, 'I like it, but I'll need to check with my director first.' What does this most likely tell the rep?

options.label: The buyer has no need for the product
The buyer wants a lower price immediately
The buyer has rejected the product outright
The buyer is not the final decision maker

rubric: Needing a director's approval signals limited authority.
It is not a rejection or a price complaint; the buyer says they like it.

items.prompt: Why should a rep qualify a lead before giving a full presentation?

options.label: Presentations only work when the buyer has already signed
Qualifying removes the need to ask discovery questions
It focuses effort on leads that are likely to buy
Qualifying makes the buyer feel obliged to purchase

rubric: Qualifying saves time by focusing on likely buyers.
It does not create obligation or replace discovery.

items.prompt: Which statement is a benefit rather than a feature of a scheduling app?

options.label: It has a mobile version and a desktop version
It syncs with three different calendar systems
It saves your team two hours of planning a week
It includes a built-in reminder tool for meetings

rubric: A benefit is the value to the buyer, such as time saved.
The others describe what the product has or does, which are features.

items.prompt: A rep skips discovery and gives every buyer the same generic pitch. What is the most likely result?

options.label: Buyers often see little relevance to their needs
Buyers feel the pitch is tailored to their situation
Buyers raise fewer objections because the pitch is simple
Buyers close faster because the pitch is shorter

rubric: Without discovery the pitch cannot address specific needs, so value looks unclear.
Faster closes or fewer objections do not follow from a generic pitch.

items.prompt: Why is it useful to track deals in a sales pipeline? Select all that apply.

options.label: It guarantees every listed deal will close
It helps estimate likely future revenue
It makes stalled deals easier to spot
It shows which stage each deal is in

rubric: A pipeline gives visibility, forecasting and stall detection.
Listing a deal never guarantees it will close.

items.prompt: After a good demo, a buyer says, 'Send me some information and I'll get back to you.' The rep has heard this before from buyers who never replied. Which interpretation and response is best?

options.label: Treat it as a rejection and remove the lead from the pipeline at once
Treat it as vague, so agree on a specific next step and date
Treat it as a firm yes and mark the deal as closed-won today
Treat it as a price objection and offer a discount to win it now

rubric: The phrase is vague and often stalls, so fixing a dated next step keeps the deal moving.
It is neither a clear yes, a clear no, nor a price objection.

items.prompt: What is the main purpose of asking discovery questions early in a sales conversation?

options.label: To collect contact details so the lead can join an email newsletter
To get the buyer to agree to the price before any demo is shown, so later talks go faster
To present every product feature to the buyer as early as possible, so nothing is missed
To uncover the buyer's problems and priorities so the offer can be tied to them

rubric: Discovery exists to learn the buyer's needs so the solution can be matched to them.
Distractors treat discovery as pitching, price-fixing or list building.

items.prompt: Why do salespeople qualify a lead before investing time in a full proposal?

options.label: To increase the number of deals shown in the pipeline report
To give every lead the same demo and the same discount offer
To focus effort on buyers with a real need, budget and authority
To prove to the buyer that the product beats every rival

rubric: Qualifying filters for need, budget and authority so time goes to likely buyers.
Distractors confuse qualifying with standardising or inflating pipeline numbers.

items.prompt: Which statement describes a benefit rather than a feature of a reporting tool?

options.label: It has a native mobile app for both iOS and Android devices
It integrates with forty other business tools through ready-made connectors
It saves your team five hours of reporting each week
It includes automated weekly reports that can be scheduled by email

rubric: A benefit states the value the buyer gets, here time saved.
The other options describe what the product has or does, which are features.

items.prompt: A buyer says, "That's too expensive." In most cases, what does this objection suggest?

options.label: The buyer has misunderstood which product is being offered
The buyer wants the rep to cut the price on the spot
The buyer has made a final refusal and will never reconsider
The buyer does not yet see enough value to justify the cost

rubric: Price objections usually signal that perceived value is lower than the price.
Distractors read it as a final no or as a pure request for a discount.

items.prompt: Which of the following is an open-ended discovery question?

options.label: Are you the person who signs contracts?
Do you currently use a CRM system?
Is your budget approved for this quarter?
How are you tracking customer renewals today?

rubric: Open questions invite explanation and cannot be answered with yes or no.
The other options are closed yes/no questions.

items.prompt: Which buyer behaviours are typically buying signals during a sales conversation? Select all that apply.

options.label: Says they are busy and will look at email next quarter
Asks about the implementation timeline and onboarding steps
Keeps steering the talk back to unrelated topics
Asks which similar companies already use the product

rubric: Questions about rollout and peer references show the buyer imagining ownership.
Postponing or deflecting signals low commitment, not buying intent.

items.prompt: A rep finishes a demo for a manager who says, "Looks interesting, just send me some information." No other meeting is planned and the rep has no other contact at the company. What does this reply most likely indicate?

options.label: Interest is unconfirmed, so agree a dated next step
A firm decision to buy, so the rep should send the contract today
A clear rejection, so the rep should close the deal as lost today
A request for a discount, so the rep should offer one right away

rubric: It is a vague, non-committal reply; the rep must confirm interest and set a next step.
Distractors over-read it as a yes, a no, or a price request.

items.prompt: A discovery call has confirmed the buyer's need, budget and who makes the decision. What is the most appropriate next step in the sales process?

options.label: Ask for a signature on the contract straight away
Return the lead to the marketing list for nurturing
Wait for the buyer to call back when ready to proceed
Prepare a demo or proposal tailored to the stated needs

rubric: A qualified lead moves on to a tailored demo or proposal.
Distractors skip stages, abandon a qualified lead or stay passive.

items.prompt: A pipeline has Deal A: $10,000 at 50% probability, Deal B: $20,000 at 25%, and Deal C: $8,000 at 75%. What is the weighted pipeline value?
rubric: $38,000 is the unweighted total; others come from averaging errors.

items.prompt: A rep works 200 leads. 25% become qualified opportunities and 20% of qualified opportunities close. How many deals should the rep expect to win?
rubric: 200 x 0.25 = 50 qualified; 50 x 0.20 = 10 deals.
Other answers apply only one rate or mix the steps.

items.prompt: A prospect says, "We already use Competitor X." Which response best applies good objection handling?

options.label: Ask what they like and what they would change about Competitor X
Thank them for their time and end the conversation politely
Offer a 30% discount before learning anything more about them
Tell them Competitor X is poor quality and they should switch

rubric: Probing the current solution reveals gaps the rep can address.
Distractors attack, give up, or discount without understanding.

items.prompt: A buyer has agreed the product covers their three main needs, asked about start dates and raised no concerns. Which closing move fits best?

options.label: Return to discovery and re-ask the earlier questions to be sure nothing was missed
Offer a bigger discount to create urgency before the buyer changes their mind
Send another case study and wait for the buyer to get back to you
Recap what was agreed and propose a specific go-live date

rubric: The buyer is ready, so a summary and assumptive close moves to a decision.
Other options delay or add unneeded concessions.

items.prompt: A rep has just finished a product demo with a qualified buyer. Which actions apply good practice at this point? Select all that apply.

options.label: Ask whether any concerns could block the decision
End by saying "let me know" and wait for a reply
Recap the needs the buyer stated and how the demo addressed them
Agree a specific next step with a date

rubric: Recapping, setting a dated next step and surfacing concerns keep the deal moving.
Leaving it open-ended hands control to the buyer and stalls the deal.

items.prompt: A rep emailed a proposal to a qualified buyer 30 days ago. The deal still sits in the proposal stage and the buyer has not replied to one reminder email. The rep wants to move the deal forward. What should the rep do next?

options.label: Send a lower-priced proposal without asking about concerns
Mark the deal as won because the buyer raised no objections
Call the buyer to ask what is blocking a decision and confirm the timeline
Email the same proposal every week with no new information

rubric: A direct conversation uncovers blockers and resets the timeline.
Distractors discount blindly, misreport the pipeline, or repeat ineffective emails.

items.prompt: A prospect says, "Your price is too high." You have not yet learned what they are comparing it to. Which response best applies sound objection handling?

options.label: List every feature again to show the price is justified
Ask what they are comparing the price to before responding
Offer a 10% discount right away to keep the deal moving
Tell them the competitors are really more expensive overall

rubric: Clarifying the basis of the objection comes before answering it, because "too high" may mean budget, a competitor quote or unclear value.
Discounting or restating features answers a problem you have not yet diagnosed.

items.prompt: A prospect has a confirmed need, a signed-off budget and the authority to buy, but says they cannot start until a contract expires in 12 months. Which pipeline action best fits?

options.label: Place it in a nurture track with a dated follow-up before renewal
Mark the lead as lost and remove all contact from the pipeline
Keep it at the top of the forecast as a likely deal this month
Move to the proposal stage and push for a close this quarter

rubric: A qualified lead with a distant timeline belongs in nurture with a planned re-engagement date.
Forcing a close or deleting the lead ignores the timeline criterion.

items.prompt: Your pipeline holds three open deals: $40,000 at 50% probability, $20,000 at 25% and $10,000 at 80%. What is the weighted forecast?
rubric: $70,000 is the unweighted total.

items.prompt: You must close 12 deals this quarter. Historically 20% of proposals close, and 40% of demos lead to a proposal. How many demos do you need to run?
rubric: 60 forgets the demo-to-proposal conversion step.

items.prompt: In discovery, a prospect tells you their team tracks customer orders in a shared spreadsheet (a situation answer). Using the SPIN approach, which question should you ask next?

options.label: Would you like to see a quick demo of how our order software works?
If we removed those order delays, how much would that save you per year?
How many people on your team use the spreadsheet each day?
How often do spreadsheet errors cause problems with orders?

rubric: After a situation answer, a problem question surfaces difficulties the buyer feels.
Implication or need-payoff questions are premature, and pitching skips discovery.

items.prompt: You are starting discovery with a new B2B prospect. Which questions apply good discovery practice? Select all that apply.

options.label: "Who else will be involved in deciding on a solution?"
"Would a tool with automated reporting be useful to your team?"
"What have you already tried to fix this?"
"Our clients usually save 20% in year one, so is that the kind of result you want?"

items.prompt: After a 15-minute first call, a prospect says, "This sounds interesting, just send me a proposal." You do not yet know their budget, their success criteria or who else must approve. What should you do next?

options.label: Ask them to email their requirements and budget, and hold the proposal until their written reply arrives
Send the proposal tonight with a deep discount, so it beats rival quotes before they finish comparing
Send your standard proposal that night, since a fast reply shows responsiveness and keeps momentum up
Offer a short call to confirm goals, budget and approvers, then send a tailored proposal

rubric: A proposal without confirmed criteria and stakeholders is likely to stall; a brief call secures them.
Sending generic or discounted proposals skips qualification.

items.prompt: Your funnel shows: lead to demo 30%, demo to proposal 10%, proposal to close 40%. The team benchmark for demo to proposal is 40%. Which diagnosis is best supported?

options.label: Reps are closing too few proposals, so closing skills and negotiation need coaching
Demos reach poorly qualified prospects or build too little value
Pricing is too high, since prospects are not accepting the proposals they receive
Lead generation is the main problem because too few leads enter the top of the funnel

rubric: The demo-to-proposal step is far below benchmark while later stages are healthy, pointing to qualification or demo value.
The other stages do not show the gap.

items.prompt: Several deals get a verbal yes from your champion, then stall for weeks in legal and procurement review. What is the most likely root cause?

options.label: The proposal price was set too low for buyers to take the offer seriously
The champion lacks enthusiasm for the product itself and is not selling it internally
The approval steps and approvers were never mapped in discovery
Buyers are deliberately using a stall tactic to gain negotiating leverage on price

rubric: Late-stage surprises usually come from not mapping the buying process and approval steps early.
Enthusiasm and price do not explain stalls after a yes.

items.prompt: A buyer says "We need to think about it" at the end of a third meeting, with no concerns raised earlier. What does this most likely signal?

options.label: The buyer wants a lower price, so a discount should be offered
An unspoken concern remains that should be uncovered before leaving
The buyer is ready to sign and just needs a few quiet days
The buyer has no interest, so the deal should be dropped from the pipeline

rubric: A vague stall usually hides an unvoiced objection; a probing question surfaces it.
Assuming readiness, price or disinterest are guesses without evidence.

items.prompt: A win/loss review finds 55% of lost deals ended in "no decision" and only 15% went to competitors. What does this most strongly suggest?

options.label: Prices are too high relative to the market in general
Competitor products are better, so the product needs more features
The cost of inaction was not made compelling enough in the sales process
Reps should offer larger discounts to beat inertia

rubric: Most losses to no decision point to weak urgency and value case rather than competition.
Features and price would show up as competitor losses.

items.prompt: A manager lets reps discount 20% freely. Close rate rose from 25% to 30%, but average deal size fell 20% and no more deals started. What does comparing the figures show?

options.label: Revenue fell, since 1.30 x 0.80 is about 1.04 only if costs are ignored
Revenue rose, since the close rate improved
Revenue rose about 4%, but margin likely fell sharply
Revenue is unchanged, because the effects offset exactly

rubric: Revenue per opportunity scales as 1.2 x 0.8 = 0.96? No: close rate rose 20% (25 to 30) and size fell 20%, giving 0.96, a slight drop in revenue and a larger margin loss.
Best choice flags that discounting trades margin for little gain.

items.prompt: Which observations are warning signs that a late-stage deal is at risk of slipping or being lost? Select all that apply.

options.label: The only contact is an end user who cannot reach the budget holder
The buyer has stopped replying to emails for two weeks
The buyer asked detailed questions about implementation timing
The close date has been pushed back twice without a stated reason

rubric: Lack of executive access, silence and unexplained date slips all signal weak commitment.
Detailed implementation questions usually indicate genuine buying interest.

items.prompt: A rep marks a deal as "commit" for next week. The only contact is a team member who loves the product; no meeting with the budget holder has occurred and no proposal has been reviewed with procurement. Which is the most telling flaw in the forecast?

options.label: The rep has not offered a discount or incentive that would pull the decision into next week's close
The deal is probably too large to close inside one quarter, whatever the buyer's approval path
The commit stage is unsupported because the economic buyer and approval steps are unconfirmed
The contact's enthusiasm makes them an unreliable source, so their feedback should be discounted entirely

rubric: A commit forecast requires confirmed access to the economic buyer and a clear approval path.
Enthusiasm, discounting and size do not address the missing evidence.

items.prompt: A pipeline review shows 40 deals in 'Proposal sent' with an average age of 70 days, against a typical 25-day cycle. Win rate from this stage is also falling. Which diagnosis best explains both patterns?

options.label: Market demand has softened this quarter, so every stage in the pipeline is slowing down in equal measure
Proposals are priced too high for the segment, so buyers delay and then finally choose a cheaper rival
Reps are not following up often enough after sending proposals, so buyers lose interest and go cold
The stage has no exit criteria tied to buyer actions, so reps park weak deals there and inflate it

rubric: Aging plus falling win rate suggests the stage holds unqualified deals because entry and exit are not defined by buyer commitments.
Follow-up, price and demand explanations would not by themselves concentrate the slowdown in one stage.

items.prompt: Inbound leads close at 30% with an average deal of 20k. Outbound leads close at 8% with an average deal of 60k and a cycle twice as long. What must an analyst compare before declaring one source better?

options.label: Expected revenue per rep-hour after cycle length and prospecting cost, since win rate ignores effort and value
Average deal size alone, because larger contracts always give more revenue however long they take to close
Number of leads generated per month, because volume decides which source keeps the pipeline reliably full
Win rate alone, because it shows which source buyers actually trust and is the cleanest measure of fit

rubric: Sources differ in win rate, size, cycle and effort, so only a combined return-on-effort view allows a fair comparison.
Single-metric answers each ignore at least one of the other drivers.

items.prompt: On a first call, before any discovery, a prospect says 'Just send me your pricing.' Which interpretation is most useful for deciding how to respond?

options.label: The buyer is uninterested and wants to end the call politely, so the rep should move the contact to nurture
The buyer is likely screening vendors on price, so sending numbers without context invites comparison; probe the need first
The buyer is ready to purchase, so sending a quote immediately will speed the deal along and show responsiveness
The buyer has authority over budget, so the rep can safely skip stakeholder mapping and go directly to negotiation

rubric: Early price requests usually signal screening, and price without value context turns the deal into a commodity comparison.
The other options read the request as buying intent, disinterest or authority without evidence.

items.prompt: Discovery surfaced three costly problems with a prospect's current vendor. Later the prospect says 'We're fairly happy with them.' What does this mismatch most likely indicate?

options.label: The pain is real but not tied to a cost of inaction or urgent event, so staying put still feels safe
The prospect is negotiating tactically, so a larger discount offered up front will resolve the objection quickly
The prospect was exaggerating earlier, so the earlier pain points should be discounted from the business case
The vendor has since fixed the problems, so the rep should ask for the new contract renewal date

rubric: Stated pain without quantified consequences or a trigger event rarely beats status-quo comfort.
Other options assume dishonesty, a vendor fix or a pricing tactic with no supporting evidence.

items.prompt: A deal slipped its close date twice. Notes show: the contact owns the problem and loves the demo, the CFO controls budget and has never been met, and legal is not yet involved. Which detail best explains the slippage?

options.label: The demo happened too early, so the buyer did not have time to compare alternatives before deciding
No access to the economic buyer means the contact cannot secure budget, and the deal waits on someone unseen
Legal has not been involved yet, so contract review is the main bottleneck delaying signature
The contact loved the demo, which means enthusiasm is hiding hidden doubts about the real fit

rubric: A champion without access to budget authority cannot close internally, so dates keep slipping.
Legal timing is normally late-stage and enthusiasm is not a cause of delay.

items.prompt: A rep forecasts a deal at 'Commit' (90%). Which findings suggest it is weaker than its stage implies? Select all that apply.

options.label: Only one contact at the buyer has engaged in the last two months of activity
Six people from the buyer attended the demo and asked detailed questions
The close date was set by the rep's quota needs, not by an event on the buyer's side
The buyer's IT team asked for an implementation timeline and named a project lead
Buyer legal has returned redlines on the draft contract and asked for a call

rubric: Single-threading and a rep-driven date show missing buyer commitment and urgency.
Redlines, implementation planning and broad attendance are normal late-stage buying signals.

items.prompt: A rep closed a mid-market customer who churned after four months. The review shows they bought mainly for Feature X, which works only with a custom integration the customer's IT team never had capacity to build. The rep had run a standard demo and then sent a proposal. Which process failure best explains the churn?

options.label: The rep did not secure a long enough contract term, so the customer had little incentive to stay committed after the first months
Discovery never validated the customer's technical capacity to realise the use case before proposing
The price was too high relative to the value delivered, so the customer felt the product was never worth the spend
Customer success failed to onboard the account properly, so the cause lies after the sale and not in the selling process

rubric: The root cause is a qualification gap: the use case depended on capacity that was never checked before the proposal.
Price, onboarding and contract length do not explain why the key feature could not be used.

items.prompt: At quarter end a buyer asks for 15% off. Policy allows reps up to 10% without approval. Criteria: protect margin, avoid training the buyer to expect discounts, close this quarter. Which response best fits?

options.label: Grant 10% now with no conditions so the deal closes quickly and the quarter target is secured
Offer 15% by asking a manager to approve it, since the buyer's request is the only number that matters
Offer up to 10% only in exchange for a signed order this quarter and a multi-year term or reference
Refuse any discount and restate value, because discounting always weakens the price position over time

rubric: Trading a limited concession for commitments meets all three criteria.
Unconditional discounts, flat refusals and exceeding policy each fail at least one stated criterion.

items.prompt: A team sells a complex platform to enterprises, with 6 to 10 stakeholders and a formal procurement process. Criteria: expose hidden risk early and forecast reliably. Which qualification approach is best?

options.label: A gut-feel rating from the rep after each call, because experienced reps sense buyer intent accurately and spot weak deals early
A budget-authority-need-timing check on the first contact, because it is quick, proven, and keeps every deal on the same simple path
A framework mapping the economic buyer, decision process, criteria and champion, since deals stall on unseen approvers
A lead score based on company size and web visits, because it can be automated and applied consistently without rep time

rubric: Multi-stakeholder deals need qualification that maps the decision process and economic buyer.
Single-contact checks, lead scores and gut feel do not surface organisational risk.

items.prompt: A rep has time for one new outreach push. Criteria: good fit, a live trigger event, and a reachable decision-maker. Account A: perfect fit, no trigger, no contact. Account B: good fit, just raised funding, VP replied. Account C: weak fit, urgent need. Account D: fair fit, big brand. Which is best?

options.label: Account B, because it meets all three criteria at once, with a trigger and an open door
Account D, because a recognisable brand creates reference value that outweighs all the other criteria
Account C, because urgent need shortens the cycle regardless of fit and speeds up the commission
Account A, because perfect fit predicts long-term value more than any short-term event can

rubric: Only Account B satisfies fit, trigger and access together.
The others each optimise one factor while failing the stated criteria.

items.prompt: A buyer says a rival is 20% cheaper. The rep replies, 'We cost more because we're simply the better product.' Which critique is most valid?

options.label: It works for price objections, since buyers usually accept a quality claim from a rep they already trust and like
It asserts superiority without linking it to the buyer's outcomes, so it gives no basis to justify the premium
It correctly defends the value, but the tone should be softer so the buyer does not feel pressured into deciding
It concedes the price gap is real, so the rep should have matched the rival's price to keep the deal moving now

rubric: Premiums are justified by quantified buyer outcomes, not generic claims of quality.
Other options misjudge the problem as tone or accept an unsupported assertion.

items.prompt: A rep has 6 months to deliver 300k of quota. Option 1: one 400k deal with a 9-month typical cycle. Option 2: three 100k-ish deals in late stage with 2-month cycles. Criteria: hit quota reliably, preserve upside. Which plan is best?

options.label: Put all effort into the 400k deal, because a single deal would exceed the quota by a wide margin
Split time equally across all four deals, so no opportunity gets neglected and risk is fully spread
Focus on closing the late-stage deals for quota and keep light-touch progress on the large deal
Drop both and prospect for new deals, since neither option is certain to succeed in six months

rubric: The large deal's cycle exceeds the window, so quota should rest on shorter deals while keeping the large one alive.
Betting everything on it, abandoning both, or splitting evenly all fail reliability or upside.

items.prompt: A champion who was responsive for weeks has gone silent for 3 weeks before a planned close date. Criteria: re-engage without discounting and without losing the relationship. Which moves are sound? Select all that apply.

options.label: Send daily check-in emails asking if the champion has had time to review the proposal
Offer an unprompted 10% discount to restart momentum before the close date passes
Reach a second stakeholder with a short note tied to the business problem the champion described
Send a candid message restating the cost of delay and offering a clear choice to proceed or pause

rubric: Multi-threading and a clear, value-based decision request re-engage without conceding price.
Daily pings add pressure without value, and unprompted discounts teach buyers that silence earns concessions.

items.prompt: A prospect asks for a free 30-day pilot. It would cost the vendor about 20 hours of services, and the sponsor has not defined success criteria or a decision date. The rep's criteria: limit unpaid effort, keep momentum, and make the pilot lead to a decision. Which response is best?

options.label: Agree to the free pilot as asked, since refusing could end the conversation and lose the deal altogether
Propose a scoped pilot with written success criteria, a decision date and a commitment to buy if they are met
Offer a longer free pilot with extra services, so the buyer sees the full value before talking about money
Decline any pilot and send a reference list instead, because pilots rarely convert to purchases

rubric: A scoped pilot with agreed criteria and a decision date limits effort and ties the pilot to a purchase decision.
Unconditional free pilots and refusals fail the effort or momentum criteria, and longer pilots increase unpaid effort.

items.prompt: Standard advice says to create urgency with an end-of-quarter discount. In which situation is that tactic most likely to backfire?

options.label: A first-time buyer with a funded project and a hard go-live date set by an executive sponsor who wants it signed
A small buyer whose single decision-maker has already confirmed budget and product fit and is ready to sign
A transactional buyer comparing two near-identical products on price in a short cycle with no switching costs
A procurement team that has learned your discounts recur each quarter and delays buying to extract them

rubric: Repeated quarter-end discounts train buyers to wait, so the tactic erodes price and creates no urgency.
Other options describe buyers with real deadlines or simple price comparisons, where the tactic is neutral or helpful.

items.prompt: Four deals of equal size are forecast to close this quarter. Judged by risk of slipping, which is the riskiest?

options.label: The economic buyer confirmed budget, and a competing vendor is in the final round on aligned pricing
The buyer asked for a reference call and a security questionnaire, and both are already scheduled
The champion is enthusiastic, but the economic buyer is unmet and legal review has not started
Procurement requested standard redlines, and both sides signed a mutual close plan with dates

rubric: Champion enthusiasm without economic-buyer access and legal progress leaves the unseen steps that cause slippage.
Other deals show buyer-side commitments and scheduled steps, so their risk is lower.

items.prompt: A rep runs discovery by reading 15 checklist questions in fixed order and rarely follows up. The goal is to uncover priorities and the decision process. Which critique is best?

options.label: The call needs more questions, since broader coverage gives the rep more data and a fuller picture to qualify the buyer
The rep should open with a product demo, because buyers reveal their real priorities faster once they see features working
The fixed order turns discovery into interrogation; following up on answers surfaces impact and decision process
The checklist should be cut to five questions, because shorter calls keep buyers engaged and produce more candid answers

rubric: Discovery quality comes from following the buyer's answers into impact and process, not from coverage or order.
Adding questions or demoing early keeps the rep in script mode and misses the stated goal.

items.prompt: A new team with little history forecasts using stage-weighted pipeline. Reps define stage progress themselves and forecasts run high. Which fix best fits the criterion of reliable forecasts?

options.label: Add more stages, because finer stage granularity lets each probability estimate track deal progress more accurately
Replace stage weights with each rep's gut-feel commit, since reps know their own deals better than the CRM stages do
Apply a flat 50% haircut to all pipeline, because a uniform correction is simple, transparent and fair to every rep
Require buyer-verified evidence to exit each stage, so probabilities reflect buyer behaviour, not rep opinion

rubric: Inflation comes from seller-defined progress, so evidence-based exit criteria fix the cause.
Gut commits and flat haircuts do not address the cause; more stages just add more self-reported steps.

items.prompt: A buyer says, 'Your price is well above the competitor's.' The goal is to protect margin and learn the real reason. Which response best meets it?

options.label: Offer a discount at once to match the competitor, so the deal keeps momentum and the objection ends
Point to your brand reputation and customer base, since trust justifies a premium to most buyers
Restate the ROI figures from the proposal and the payback period, because repeating value overcomes a price objection
Ask what is being compared and what the cheaper quote covers, since price gaps often hide scope gaps

rubric: Probing the comparison reveals whether the objection is price or scope before any concession.
Discounting or repeating pitches answers an unverified objection and risks margin.

items.prompt: A team applies BANT (budget, authority, need, timeline) rigidly to complex B2B deals with buying committees. Which are valid criticisms of that rigid use? Select all that apply.

options.label: Qualification adds no value on large deals, so it should be skipped in favour of demos
Timeline is irrelevant to forecasting, so it should be dropped from qualification
Budget often does not exist until value is shown, so a 'no budget' answer wrongly disqualifies deals
Authority is spread across a committee, so asking for one decision-maker misreads how deals are approved
Buyers may not yet recognise their need, so a stated-need test filters out deals that discovery could create

rubric: Rigid BANT misfires when budget is created later, authority is shared and needs are unrecognised.
Timeline matters for forecasting, and skipping qualification is not a valid conclusion.

items.prompt: Three weeks before quarter end, a rep's champion says, 'We love it, it's a done deal,' but keeps declining to introduce the CFO, who must sign off. The rep has discount authority. Which action is the best judgment?

options.label: Propose a joint plan with a CFO meeting; say it can't be committed without it
Offer the champion a 10% discount if they get a signature before quarter end, so urgency replaces the need for CFO access
Email the CFO directly without telling the champion, since time is short and the access gap is putting the quarter at risk
Keep the deal in commit and wait for the champion to return, because pushing for the CFO may damage the rapport built so far

rubric: Securing economic-buyer access through a transparent joint plan tests the champion's real influence and protects forecast integrity.
Discounting, bypassing or waiting leave the unseen sign-off risk unaddressed or damage trust.

items.prompt: Design a closing approach for a 90-day deal with a six-person buying committee. Constraints: no discount, late-stage blockers must surface early, and no pressure tactics. Which design meets all three?

options.label: A final proposal with an expiry date sent after the last demo, so the committee sees a clear deadline and decides on schedule
An assumptive close in the last meeting, with the contract circulated on the spot so the committee treats signing as the natural next step
An early verbal commitment from the sponsor, with contract and security paperwork handled afterwards by the buyer's own teams
A mutual close plan with the champion listing legal, security and procurement steps with owners and dates, reviewed weekly

rubric: A co-built plan with dated buyer-side steps exposes blockers early without discounts or pressure.
The other designs rely on deadlines, assumption or deferral, which add pressure or hide blockers.

items.prompt: Design a prospecting approach for 200 named target accounts with a high contract value and a small team. Constraints: messages must be relevant, and multiple roles per account must be reached. Which plan fits?

options.label: Research each account, contact three roles with messages tied to a trigger event, and mix email, phone and referrals
Buy a larger contact list covering every employee at the accounts and cold-call each person once, to maximise conversations
Load all 200 accounts into one automated email sequence with the same template, weekly follow-ups and open-rate tracking
Post product content on social channels each week, then wait for the target accounts' buyers to respond inbound

rubric: Account-level research, multi-threading and trigger-based messages satisfy relevance and multi-role constraints at low volume.
Template blasts, one-touch calls and passive posting fail the relevance or reach constraints.

items.prompt: Define pipeline stage exit criteria so that forecasts are reliable even when reps are optimistic. Which design satisfies that?

options.label: Stages end on a buyer action, such as the economic buyer confirming the problem and sponsor in writing
Stages end when the deal age passes a set number of days, so old deals move forward automatically
Stages end when the rep has completed an activity, such as sending a proposal or running a demo
Stages end when the manager approves the rep's judgment that the deal is progressing well

rubric: Buyer-verifiable exit criteria remove reliance on rep optimism.
Activity, opinion and age-based criteria are seller-controlled and do not reflect buyer commitment.

items.prompt: A deal is stalled in 'no decision'. The buyer agrees there is a problem but has never quantified its cost. Constraints: no discount and no new demos. Which plan best fits?

options.label: Build a cost-of-inaction model with the buyer's own data and have the sponsor present it internally
Schedule another product demo for the wider team, so more stakeholders see the value
Ask the champion to sign now and promise to adjust the contract terms after the first month
Send a final offer with a deadline, so the buyer must decide before the price changes

rubric: Quantifying inaction with buyer data gives the sponsor an internal case and attacks the cause of stalling.
Deadlines, extra demos and loose terms violate constraints or fail to address the unquantified cost.

items.prompt: A proposed discovery plan for enterprise deals covers pain, budget, timeline and competitors. Which element is most critically missing for multi-stakeholder deals?

options.label: Two or three pricing options with discount tiers, ready to present in the first meeting
A list of reference customers in the buyer's industry to name early in the first call
How the buyer approved past purchases, and who can block or influence the decision
A longer feature list, with demo scripts matched to each stakeholder's job title

rubric: Understanding the decision process and potential blockers is the key gap in enterprise discovery.
Features, pricing and references support later stages but do not reveal how the decision is made.

items.prompt: Plan a negotiation that must protect price and still close. Which elements should the plan include? Select all that apply.

options.label: A map of the buyer's non-price priorities, such as terms and timing, to use as trade items
A target and walk-away point set before the meeting, so concessions stay within limits
Disclosure of your quota deadline to show openness, so the buyer helps you close
Trades structured as give-gets, so every concession is tied to something from the buyer
An early unconditional concession to build goodwill before the buyer asks for anything

rubric: Give-gets, pre-set limits and non-price trade items protect price while enabling agreement.
Unconditional concessions and revealing deadlines hand the buyer leverage.

items.prompt: After moving upmarket, a team's win rate fell from 25% to 15%. Reps still run a demo-first process with one contact per account. The fix must show results within two quarters and add no headcount. Which redesign fits best?

options.label: Replace demo-first with multi-threaded discovery and mutual plans, require economic-buyer access at mid-stage, and coach live calls
Add product training so reps can run longer demos covering more features, answer technical committee questions, and handle detailed security reviews
Raise outbound volume and add sequences to more target accounts, so absolute wins return to earlier levels even at the lower win rate
Cut prices and offer larger discounts on big deals, so the higher contract value no longer slows buyers' decisions or stalls approvals

rubric: The drop stems from a single-threaded, demo-first process mismatched to committee deals; the redesign fixes it within the constraints.
More volume, discounts or training leave the process mismatch in place.
